title: The problem with aiming for average

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At 18 years old, Todd Rose was regarded as academically weak because his grades were consistently low. He went on to do a series of minimum-wage jobs in factories, retail stores and call centres. Rose says that no matter what he tried, everything ended in disaster. Now, at 42, Rose is the director of the Mind, Brain and Education programme at Harvard Graduate School of Education, which gives him a sense of fulfilment and achievement. However, he admits that he often felt extremely worried and stressed about his future. So what happened? ‘I'd like to say | was smart and figured it out,’ he says. ‘In reality, it was desperation,’ Eventually, he stopped trying to follow the path that everyone else was following and instead, he created a pathway that suited his way of learning. As he climbed the career ladder, there was an element of luck involved, too, when he met people who became mentors. But Rose believes the real key to his success was a shift in thinking.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Rose has recently been asking people to question the assumptions we make, about ourselves and others, that limit our potential. The enemy is what he calls ‘averagarianism’, The notion of the ‘average man’ emerged in the early 19th century when the academic discipline of statistics was first developed. It was astrologers that gave this new science its name, but then a Belgian mathematician, Adolphe Quetelet, saw it might be useful in measuring the irregular patterns of complex social phenomena such as crime or marriage rates. Quetelet calculated the average of various human attributes: chest circumferences, weight, height and so on. To him, the average represented perfection.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the late 1800s, Frederick Winslow Taylor took Quetelet's views further. A pioneer of management consultancy, his vision for greater efficiency in the industrialised US was that businesses, rather than encouraging employees’ talents, should hire average men who fitted the system. Taylor believed there was only one way to accomplish any process: the standardised way, and his philosophy still powers businesses today. Rose had personal experience of this ‘averagarianism’ while working in a call centre and an aluminium factory. Here, he found he was a cog in a machine, a worker expected to conform to the average, with no opportunity to show initiative or use his individual talents.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: As the world became increasingly standardised, ‘averagarian' ideas were embraced by social policy makers, educators and politicians, and remain a powerful force, influencing the design of institutions and how we measure human potential and performance. The assumptions are that the average represents most of us, and the way we deviate from it defines us; the ideal is to be better than average at everything. ‘I don't think most of us are aware of the impact this has on our lives,’ says Rose. But averages are a constant feature for the media: average house prices, average student debt, average earnings. More critically, the way we are evaluated academically or ranked in the workplace is based around how closely we approximate to the average or how far we can exceed it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Rose doesn't accept this approach. He believes we should recognise that we all have something unique to offer, and adapt our systems accordingly. He has a few ideas, based on his experience of tapping into his full potential while at college. On discovering that his academic counsellor at Weber State University had made much the same course recommendations to another student with a very different background, Rose decided to structure his study to suit his areas of interest, strengths and weaknesses. He chose to take the most interesting courses in the first two years because he knew they would hold his attention. He played to his own personal preferences by signing up for classes involving discussion, rather than long lectures. By the time the duller study came along, he had developed his learning skills, and graduated with straight As.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Without realising it, Rose had designed his higher education around some basic beliefs: first, talent is ‘jagged’: we are good at some things, and not so great at others; second, the context principle: our behaviour is not determined solely by our traits, but also influenced by the situation we find ourselves in; and third, the pathway principle, which states there are no fixed ladders of development in any area of our lives but rather multiple ways to reach the same outcome. Rose thinks higher education should be directed by those principles. He dismisses traditional structured courses, grades and diplomas, arguing for an individualised approach allowing students to determine their own education pathway. But as he points out, most universities are merely ‘caretakers of the “averagarianism” system they inherited’, which assumes students should learn a given amount of information in a given time. But if universities took a more flexible approach, students could demonstrate that they had the expertise and knowledge necessary for the career they intended to pursue.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: No-one is average, according to science. For instance, when neuroscientist Michael Miller did MRI scans of brains, he observed that no two shared the same pattern of activity when memory was being tested. This goes against traditional thinking. Psychologist Karen Adolph’s work has disproved the widely-held belief that we all follow a similar learning path to walking in our early years. Averages don’t work for sport, either. Rose notes that head coach Isiah Thomas selected basketball players for the New York Knicks on the basis of the average number of points they scored per game: then the team hit a four-year losing streak. Thomas had overlooked the fact that basketball skills are multi-dimensional, and being good at scoring doesn't mean a player will excel at all aspects of the game. The paradox is that strong teamwork requires individuality, something Thomas came to learn and which Rose hopes more people will also recognise.
